summary: This RFC reproduces the draft ISO connectionless network protocol, roughly comparable to the DoD Internet Protocol, as then being voted on in ISO. It is for information only and does not specify an ARPA Internet standard. It was replaced by RFC 994.

eli5.summary: This is a copy of another group's draft rules for sending data packets without setting up a call first, much like IP does.

questions: what is iso connectionless network protocol
subtitle: The ISO's connectionless network protocol specification, equivalent to the DoD Internet Protocol.

tldr.problem: The ISO and the DoD Internet community each developed network-layer protocols for connectionless transmission. ISO needed its own standard for interoperability with systems using the OSI model.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 926 reproduces the text of ISO DIS 8473 (Draft International Standard), which defines a connectionless network protocol with routing, segmentation, addressing, and error reporting functions similar to IP.
tldr.outcome: This protocol was later superseded by RFC 994, and neither the ISO protocol nor the DoD's Internet Protocol became the dominant standard; instead, the Internet Protocol evolved and eventually became the basis for all networks.

today: RFC 926 is Historic and documents an ISO draft standard from 1984. The ISO CLNP protocol was later superseded by RFC 994 and ultimately was not widely deployed. The Internet Protocol (IP) became the standard for worldwide networking instead. This RFC is preserved for historical record of standards development efforts.

sections.title: Introduction and History
sections.content:
This RFC reproduces the text of ISO DIS 8473 (Draft International Standard), the ISO's specification for a connectionless-mode network protocol. The document was typed in December 1984 from the May 1984 draft ISO standard during a period when ISO was voting on it as an international standard.

The protocol fills the same role as the DoD Internet Protocol in a different context. Rather than a new ARPA Internet standard, it represents how the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) approached the design of a network layer for open systems interconnection (OSI). The protocol provides connectionless transmission of data across interconnected subnetworks, with routing, segmentation, reassembly, and error reporting functions.

This document is informational and does not specify an ARPA Internet standard. It was prepared to make the ISO draft available to the Internet community for information purposes.
sections.eli5: Back in the 1980s, two big groups (ISO in Europe and the US Internet people) were designing network rules. This is what ISO came up with. It was like IP but for a different computer system.

sections.title: Addressing and Network Architecture
sections.content:
The protocol operates over interconnected subnetworks, which may be homogeneous or heterogeneous (the same or different types). A Network Entity is a system that implements the protocol; End Systems are application hosts, while Intermediate Systems (relays) forward packets between subnetworks.

Network Service Access Point Addresses (NSAPs) identify endpoints of the service. These are analogous to IP addresses. Subnetwork addresses identify attachment points to individual subnetworks and are defined separately for each subnetwork type.

The protocol is designed as a Subnetwork Independent Convergence Protocol: it works the same way over any type of subnetwork, minimizing the need for subnetwork-specific adaptations. Where subnetwork-specific functions are needed, optional Subnetwork Dependent Convergence Protocols provide mapping.

The protocol defines two simplified subsets: the Inactive Network Layer Protocol for systems connected by a single subnetwork, and the non-segmenting subset for use when subnetwork packet sizes are known to be large enough that data never needs to be split.
sections.eli5: The protocol needs to know where to send messages (an address) and what kind of network it is crossing. Unlike some systems that are tied to one type of wire, this one is flexible and works over any kind of network. And if you know things about your network in advance, you can simplify the rules.

sections.title: Protocol Data Units and Core Functions
sections.content:
The protocol exchanges Protocol Data Units (PDUs): structured packets with a header and data. Two main PDU types exist: Data PDUs (DT) for user data, and Error Report PDUs (ER) for reporting problems.

Each PDU header has several parts. The fixed part contains the protocol identifier, version, lifetime (in 500-millisecond units), flags, and type code. The address part holds the source and destination NSAP addresses. The segmentation part (when needed) tracks which segment this is and the total length for reassembly. The options part carries optional features like source routing, padding, and security. Finally, the data part carries the user payload.

The protocol performs several key functions: PDU composition (building outgoing packets), routing (choosing the next hop), segmentation (splitting large packets to fit subnetwork sizes), reassembly (reconstructing original data from segments), error reporting (notifying senders of delivery failures), and lifetime control (discarding old packets).

Each initial PDU receives a Data Unit Identifier to track its segments across the network. The Lifetime field starts at a value set by the originator and decreases as the PDU is forwarded; when it reaches zero, the PDU is discarded to prevent looping.
sections.eli5: Packets have a header with an address, a lifetime countdown, and optional extras. As they hop through the network, the countdown decreases. If a packet is too big for some networks it crosses, it gets split up and reassembled at the destination. If something goes wrong, the packet sender gets an error message.

sections.title: Routing and Forwarding Operations
sections.content:
When a PDU arrives at a network entity, the header format analysis function determines whether it has reached its destination or must be forwarded. If the destination address matches a Network Service Access Point served by the entity, the PDU is delivered to the application; otherwise, it must be forwarded.

The route PDU function uses the destination NSAP address, quality of service parameters, and potentially other information to determine which subnetwork and intermediate system should receive the PDU next. This is the routing decision.

If a PDU is too large for the chosen subnetwork's maximum packet size, the segmentation function splits the PDU into smaller derived PDUs, each marked with the original Data Unit Identifier, a segment offset, and the total length. All segments must be reassembled at the destination before delivery to the application.

The forward PDU function transmits the packet (or segment) to the next hop. Quality of service parameters are preserved and passed to the subnetwork service. The PDU lifetime control function decrements the lifetime field; if it reaches zero before a PDU can be forwarded, the PDU is discarded and an error report is generated.
sections.eli5: The network looks at each packet's destination. If it is for this computer, it gets handed to the application. Otherwise, the network figures out which neighbor to send it to. If the packet is too big for that network, it gets chopped into pieces, tagged so they can be glued back together later, and each piece is sent separately. As packets travel, a counter ticks down. If the counter hits zero, the packet gets thrown away to prevent it from wandering the network forever.

sections.title: Service Model and Quality of Service
sections.content:
The protocol provides a Network Service to applications above it, using primitives for unitdata (datagram) transmission. The N_UNITDATA request primitive asks the network to send data to a destination; the N_UNITDATA indication primitive delivers received data to an application. Both carry parameters including source address, destination address, quality of service, and user data.

The protocol assumes a connectionless Subnetwork Service from the layer below, using similar SN_UNITDATA primitives. The maximum NSDU (Network Service Data Unit) size is 64,512 octets, though subnetwork-specific limits may be smaller and trigger segmentation.

Quality of Service (QOS) parameters include transit delay, protection against unauthorized access, cost determinants, priority, and residual error probability. The protocol carries these parameters from the application down to the subnetwork service, and subnetwork providers attempt to honor them when possible.

If a subnetwork cannot deliver at the requested QOS, the subnetwork provider attempts delivery at whatever QOS is available—this is a local matter for each subnetwork type. Error reporting allows the originator to be informed if delivery fails.
sections.eli5: Applications ask the network "please send this data there" and say how important it is (should it be fast? should it be private?). The network promises to do its best, but if the network is not good enough, it still sends the data anyway. Networks inside can make their own decisions about priorities and tradeoffs.

sections.title: Optional Features and Extensions
sections.content:
The protocol supports several optional features, most carried in the options part of the PDU header. Source routing allows the originator to specify a sequence of intermediate systems the PDU must visit, enabling explicit path control. Route recording allows the PDU to note the path it takes as it travels, providing feedback to the originator.

Security options can be carried in PDU headers. The protocol preserves a security option from the incoming PDU when sending an error report, so that the error response can be secured the same way.

Padding can be added to PDUs to align them to subnetwork requirements or to obscure the true data length.

The protocol also supports error reporting. When a PDU cannot be delivered (due to lifetime expiry, lack of route, security violations, or other reasons), the receiving entity generates an Error Report PDU and sends it back to the source address. The error report identifies the reason for discard and includes data from the original PDU for correlation.

PDU checksums protect the header from corruption. A checksum is computed over the header fields (excluding the checksum field itself) and verified by each entity handling the PDU; corruption is detected and may trigger discarding or error reporting depending on implementation.
sections.eli5: Packets can carry special instructions like "follow this exact path" or "keep a log of which computers you visited." They can include security marks and padding for privacy. If something goes wrong, an error message gets sent back. The header is protected by a checksum so broken packets are detected.

fields.name: Network Layer Protocol Identifier
fields.desc: Identifies the protocol; ISO CLNP uses specific values.

fields.name: Length Indicator
fields.desc: Length of the fixed header part.

fields.name: PDU Lifetime
fields.desc: Remaining lifetime in 500ms units; decremented at each hop.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Segmentation permitted, more segments, error report.

fields.name: Type Code
fields.desc: PDU type: Data (0x1C) or Error Report (0x1D).
